title: Fair in Mind, Fair in Action: The IRIS Benchmark
one_liner: A benchmark that measures fairness across both understanding and generation in multimodal models by aggregating 60 metrics into three unified dimensions.
lead: Multimodal models (models that read both images and text) often treat different groups of people unfairly — some groups get worse answers than others. But fairness itself is a slippery idea: people disagree about what fair means. The IRIS Benchmark solves this by collecting 60 different fairness measurements into three core dimensions, letting you see exactly where and how a model fails to treat everyone equally.

paras: Multimodal models — systems that understand both images and text together — are being used everywhere: hiring, medicine, housing, hiring. When a model sees a person's face or name, it should give the same quality answer no matter who they are. But it does not.

The trouble: philosophers and researchers have dozens of different ideas about what fairness means. Some think it means equal accuracy across all groups. Some think it means the model should make the same kinds of mistakes. Some think it means the model should ignore demographic information entirely. These ideas contradict each other — you cannot satisfy all of them at once.

Worse: multimodal models have multiple failure points. A model might be fair when reading an image but unfair when writing text. Or it might treat a group fairly on one task but unfairly on another. There is no unified way to measure and fix these problems.

callout.html: The IRIS Benchmark collects 60 fairness measurements into three unified dimensions, so you can see exactly where a multimodal model fails to treat different groups equally.

panels.title: 1. One model, many groups

panels.title: 2. The fairness tangle
panels.viz_args: 60 different fairness ideas all pulling in different directions
panels.caption: 60+ different fairness metrics exist, but many contradict each other. Which one do you measure?

panels.title: 3. IRIS: three unified dimensions
panels.caption: IRIS collapses 60 metrics into three dimensions: perfect fairness, practical fairness, and how easily fixed.

panels.title: 4. Measure both ways
panels.caption: The benchmark tests fairness when the model reads images and when it writes descriptions.

panels.title: 5. Uncover the gaps
panels.caption: Diagnoses emerge: generation gaps, personality splits, counter-stereotype reward biases.

steps.text: Start with any model that reads images and text.

steps.b: Run it on diverse demographic groups
steps.text: Test the same tasks across people of different ages, genders, ethnicities, etc.
Measure accuracy, consistency, and bias using 60 different definitions of fairness.
Project all 60 metrics into three core fairness dimensions: ideal, real-world, steerability.
Identify specific patterns like generation gaps and personality splits that reveal systemic biases.

paras: Instead of picking one fairness metric and hoping it captures what you care about, IRIS measures 60 metrics simultaneously and aggregates them into three unified dimensions. This lets you see fairness trade-offs instead of pretending they do not exist.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: fairness in three dimensions
hidden.name: IRIS fairness score (high-dimensional)
paras: IRIS does not use a single fairness number. Instead, it measures fairness in three directions at once: Ideal Fairness (how far from perfect), Real-world Fidelity (how fairness works in actual use), and Bias Inertia & Steerability (how hard it is to fix). Each dimension summarizes roughly 20 of the 60 underlying metrics.

The paper computes this by running the model on diverse demographic groups, collecting ground-truth labels (what the correct answer is for each person), and then comparing what the model outputs to the ground truth for each group and dimension. A heat map shows which combinations of people and dimensions have the biggest fairness gaps.

heat.caption: Darker means bigger fairness gap. Red border highlights systemic failures in generation and counter-stereotype bias.

reads.html: Imagine a simple score from 0 to 100 for how fairly a model treats a specific group on a specific task. Darker cells here mean lower scores, i.e., more bias.
IRIS aggregates the 60 granular metrics via dimensionality reduction into the three IRIS dimensions, computed per demographic group and per understanding/generation task.

paras: The core insight: most fairness metrics measure the same deep idea but in different ways. If you measure accuracy on group A versus group B, or if you measure whether the model makes the same type of error for both groups, or whether the model gives consistent confidence — you are circling around the same core problem, just from different angles. IRIS combines these 60 angles into three directions that matter most: How far from perfect? How fair in real use? How fixable?

This works because fairness trade-offs are real. You cannot optimize for all 60 metrics at once without contradicting yourself. But you CAN optimize for the three dimensions and tell a coherent story: this model is close to ideal on some groups but fails badly on intersections (people in multiple marginalized groups), and the failure is because of a systematic bias in generation (writing descriptions) rather than understanding (reading images).

stages.s: Group metrics by shared fairness concept

math.h2: How to score fairness in three dimensions
math.words: Aggregate 60 metrics into 3 dimensions using weighted averaging; then compute disparity (difference) between groups.
math.equation: IRIS_d(g) = mean(M_g ∩ dimension_d) for group g and dimension d; Disparity(g1, g2) = abs(IRIS_d(g1) - IRIS_d(g2))
symbols: fairness score for group g on dimension d
all 60 fairness metrics applied to group g
one of three fairness directions (ideal, real-world, or fixable)
difference in fairness between two groups

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a model is tested on two groups: people with light skin and people with dark skin.
20 metrics measure accuracy fairness. For light-skin group: scores are 85, 88, 82, 90... average = 86. For dark-skin group: 72, 68, 71, 69... average = 70.
Disparity in accuracy fairness = abs(86 - 70) = 16 points.
20 other metrics measure generation fairness. Light: average 84. Dark: average 62. Disparity = 22 points.
The generation disparity is bigger, so the model is less fair at writing text than reading images.

math.note: The three IRIS dimensions let you see which kinds of fairness failures matter most instead of averaging over all 60 metrics and losing the diagnosis.

charts.title: Baseline model (unfair)
charts.note: Many gaps between demographic groups; biases are baked in.

charts.title: After IRIS diagnosis
charts.note: Once you identify which groups and tasks have the biggest disparities, you can apply targeted interventions like reweighting training data for under-served groups or modifying generation rules for specific demographics. This works because you concentrate your fixes exactly where they help most, instead of spreading fixes thinly across all groups.

items.html: The 60 metrics contradict each other by design. Optimizing for Ideal Fairness might hurt Real-world Fidelity. The IRIS approach acknowledges this trade-off instead of pretending it does not exist.
Fairness for women is not the same as fairness for women from a specific ethnicity. IRIS detects intersectional gaps (personality splits) but needs many data samples to measure them reliably.
If the training data for the model was biased, IRIS will measure that bias faithfully — but it cannot fix it. The benchmark diagnoses; you have to fix the training.

Use IRIS to identify which dimensions and demographic groups have the largest gaps, then run targeted debiasing on those groups and dimensions rather than trying to improve everything at once, because a blanket fix spreads your limited retraining budget thinly but a focused fix concentrates effort on the worst disparities.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Download a pretrained multimodal model (e.g., CLIP, LLaVA). Run it on a small dataset with images labeled by demographic group (skin tone, gender, age). Compute 10 fairness metrics manually: accuracy per group, confidence per group, and consistency across repeated captions. Visualize these 10 metrics in a 3D scatter plot, with one axis per IRIS dimension. Show how different models (and different training techniques) cluster in different regions of this fairness space.
demo.metric_eq: Disparity = max_fairness_score - min_fairness_score across groups; smaller is more fair.
demo.closing: The demo makes it impossible to miss that fairness is not one number but a trade-off space (because the 60 metrics contradict each other), and that different models fail in systematically different ways (because their training data and architecture choices push them toward different demographic groups and tasks).
